Learning article · authored 7 September 2026 · approximately 12 minutes. This explains an independent mathematical reference, not a public gffx shading implementation.

In this article

  1. A surface has a light budget
  2. Radiance, irradiance and angles
  3. What a BRDF describes
  4. Why Lambert has a pi
  5. How we accidentally created light
  6. The revised budget
  7. Testing the mathematics and the calculation
  8. Point lights and distant lights
  9. Spherical harmonics and approximation error

1. A surface has a light budget

Imagine sending 100 units of light energy onto a non-emitting surface. Some can leave as a sharp reflection, some as a broad, matte reflection, and some can be absorbed. They cannot add up to 140 units. We are describing steady reflection, not a lamp, fluorescence or stored energy being released.

“Energy conserving” means the reflected total never exceeds the incoming total. It does not mean every surface reflects everything. A dark surface is allowed to absorb most of its light. An individual bright highlight is also allowed: concentration into a narrow direction is not the same as creating energy.

2. Radiance, irradiance and angles

Radiance describes directional light: how much travels along a direction per projected area and per solid angle. Its units are watts per square metre per steradian. Irradiance is all the arriving power per surface area, summed over directions, in watts per square metre.

A solid angle is an area on a unit sphere, measured in steradians. A hemisphere contains all directions above a flat surface. The surface normal N is its perpendicular unit vector. L points from the surface toward the incoming light; V points toward the viewer. These arrows must be in the same coordinate system.

Facing light head-on gives a cosine of one. Tilting spreads the same beam over more surface area, so less power lands per unit area. At a right angle the cosine is zero. For this discussion, directions below the surface are excluded; this is separate from any two-sided material rule.

The integral means “add contributions from every incoming direction.” The cosine is part of the physical projected-area weighting, not a brightness adjustment chosen for appearance.

3. A BRDF describes directional reflection

A bidirectional reflectance distribution function, or BRDF, connects an incoming direction to an outgoing direction. Write it as f(V,L). It has units of inverse steradians. It is not itself a percentage and may be larger than one in a narrow highlight; the integrated reflected energy is what must be bounded.

For the reciprocal reflection models here, exchanging V and L leaves the BRDF unchanged. This is called reciprocity. Checking it catches corrections that behave differently when light and viewer exchange places.

A white-furnace test places the material in a uniform environment with incident radiance one. For a reciprocal non-emitting BRDF, the cosine-weighted hemisphere integral must not exceed one. The test checks energy accounting, not whether a material resembles measured skin or a particular renderer.

4. Why Lambert includes 1/pi

Lambert is an ideal matte reflection model. Its BRDF is independent of light and viewing direction. Albedo A is the reflected fraction, between zero and one in each linear colour channel.

Derivation: where does pi come from?

Let theta run from the normal to the horizon and phi around the normal. The solid-angle element is sin(theta) d-theta d-phi. Multiplying it by the projected-area cosine and integrating gives pi:

Using A instead of A/pi with the same physical lighting units would return pi times too much energy. A legacy renderer may absorb that factor into its light convention; mixing conventions is the error.

5. How we accidentally created light

We also want a glossy component. Our proposed specular term uses GGX for the distribution of tiny surface orientations, correlated Smith visibility for masking and shadowing, and Schlick Fresnel for angle-dependent reflection. Call that whole specular BRDF s. F0 is its normal-incidence Fresnel reflectance, not an arbitrary brightness multiplier. Perceptual roughness r maps to the GGX width alpha=r squared.

Our first mixture attenuated Lambert by this local Fresnel value and then added s. That sounds plausible, but the local Fresnel factor is not the total specular energy over the hemisphere.

Worked example: a failed light budget

At white albedo, F0=0.04, roughness=0.2 and view cosine=0.1, independent integration gave 1.42787 out for one unit of incident environment radiance—about 42.8 percent too much. The reference was refined before we attributed the failure to the model. We did not clamp the result or increase the allowable energy threshold.

6. Give both components the same budget

First integrate the specular BRDF to determine its directional reflected fraction E(V). Here E means a dimensionless energy fraction, not the irradiance I used earlier. Let E-average be its cosine-weighted mean over the hemisphere, divided by pi. T(V)=1-E(V) is the remaining fraction.

Proof: no double-counting, and reciprocity survives

When integrating over L, A and E(V) are constant. The integral of (1-E(L)) times the cosine is pi times (1-E-average), which cancels the denominator. The matte contribution is therefore A(1-E(V)).

The product of the two residual factors is unchanged when V and L swap, so the coupling is reciprocal. If the average residual is exactly zero, the matte term is defined as zero rather than evaluating 0/0. This proof assumes exact integrals; approximate tables still need numerical tests.

Try the budget

This simple calculator illustrates the accounting identity, not a live GGX renderer or a measured material.

E=0.30; A=0.50; glossy 0.30 + matte 0.35 = 0.65 reflected; 0.35 absorbed.

With our revised formula, the original counterexample gives 1.00003 at the refined grid. That tiny excess is within the declared numerical tolerance, not literal exact conservation by floating-point code. The coupled matte model is physically plausible and empirical: it is not an exact coating simulation, a Blender Principled replica, or a demonstrated skin-scattering model.

7. Test the calculation as well as the mathematics

An integral is continuous; a computer samples it. A narrow highlight may fit between sample locations. We therefore compare coarse and fine calculations, and use two different parameterizations for the specular integral: direct light-hemisphere integration and visible-normal integration.

The declared sweep contains 108 combinations of roughness, F0, view angle and albedo. At the recorded revision the maximum white-albedo error is 0.000225413; the maximum coarse/fine change is 0.000362298. The upper energy bound remains 1.001 and the refinement change must stay below 0.001. These finite cases do not prove every roughness, angle, device or implementation correct.

Gradients need their own checks. When fitting roughness or F0, their effects on E and E-average must also be differentiated. Our current diagnostic detaches those integrals; it is not a public, fully differentiable material implementation. The practical runtime evaluator is still to be designed.

Try it yourself

If specular reflection uses 0.3 of the budget and matte albedo is 0.5, how much is reflected and how much is absorbed?

Answer

The remaining budget is 0.7. Matte reflection uses half of that, 0.35, so total reflection is 0.65 and absorption is 0.35. The calculator above checks this accounting identity, not a complete GGX integration.

Continue learning through the textbook contents and chapter navigation.

8. Point lights and distant lights

A distant light sends parallel rays: moving a surface does not change the light's specified strength. A point source spreads its power over larger areas as you move away. Double the distance and the same power is distributed across four times the area. Radiant intensity describes the source's power per solid angle; normal-incidence irradiance describes arriving power per perpendicular area. These are not interchangeable meanings for a number called brightness.

The material still multiplies W by its BRDF and the positive normal-light cosine once. A zero distance has no defined direction and infinite ideal falloff: our planned M1 query returns an invalid mask and zero payload for that pair. This is not a physically dark lamp. Consumers must keep the mask. No hidden epsilon turns a coincident lamp into a large finite number. Normals and explicit light directions are normalized as part of these M1 recipes; this does not change the older renderer's separate arithmetic convention.

Worked example

For intensity 4, a point one unit away receives weight 4. At two units it receives 1; at half a unit it receives 16. A distant light configured to 4 remains 4. These are weights before the surface cosine and the material, not final displayed pixel values. Keep coordinate units consistent.

9. Spherical harmonics: nine knobs per color

An environment can illuminate a surface from every direction. Storing a full image of the surrounding world is one representation. A low-order spherical-harmonic expansion instead stores weights of smooth patterns over the sphere, much as a few musical harmonics approximate a complicated waveform. Band two has nine coefficients for red, nine for green and nine for blue: 27 numbers per environment. Coefficients may be negative because the basis patterns themselves have positive and negative regions.

Our first-order basis uses y, z, x in that order. Other renderers may use different signs, order or pre-scaled coefficients. Copying 27 numbers between them without converting conventions can produce plausible but wrong illumination. Batch B, sample point P and coefficient K are distinct axes: [B,P,3] normals paired with [B,9,3] coefficients produce [B,P,3] irradiance. Shared coefficients explicitly use a singleton batch or [9,3]; no hidden mixing of different scenes is allowed.

Worked example

For unit constant radiance, set the first coefficient to sqrt(4pi) in each channel and the rest to zero. Irradiance becomes pi in every direction; multiplying by white Lambert 1/pi returns one. A sharp directional source is different. Its band-two approximation has this response:

At t=1 it returns 17/16 rather than one. At t=-1 it returns 1/16 rather than zero. At t=-8/15 it is -19/480: slight negative ringing. We preserve signed results rather than clamping them and silently changing their derivatives. A fitted nonnegative environment needs an explicit constraint or different representation. The demo colors negative areas magenta while retaining actual signed values in its graph.

Try it yourself

If the point-source intensity doubles while distance doubles, does the received weight stay constant? Can nine coefficients exactly reproduce the hard light boundary?

Answer

The weight halves: twice the intensity divided by four times the squared-distance factor. No: nine smooth basis functions approximate the hard boundary. Its overshoot and negative ringing are properties to measure, not evidence that an exact directional-light formula should return negative light.

The high-resolution lighting study

Light reveals form adds a reciprocal Phong highlight to the development presentation. For unit normal N, source direction L and view V, reflect L as R=2(N dot L)N-L. Its lobe is max(R dot V,0) raised to exponent 72, scaled by 73/(2*pi). The unweighted positive-lobe integral is at most 2*pi/73; multiplying by the incident cosine cannot increase it. A 0.12 highlight budget plus 0.88 diffuse budget with albedo at most one therefore has a conservative unit energy bound. Reciprocity follows because R(L) dot V equals R(V) dot L. Numerical hemisphere integration and reciprocity tests exercise the same helper used for the images.

This is a deliberately bounded demonstration recipe, not the pending public principled material. The background, tone mapping and edge smoothing are presentation choices; no shadow solver or indirect illumination is claimed. The source bunny receives one offline display refinement, not a newly implemented public subdivision operation.

From light to surface response: five building blocks

Prerequisites: dot products, unit directions, radiance versus irradiance, and the energy-budget discussion above. A BRDF says how strongly a surface redirects light between two directions. It is not an image, a light, or a shadow test. The renderer still multiplies the incident light weight and surface cosine once.

1. Matte reflection and the half-vector

Lambert has a direction-independent BRDF: albedo divided by pi. Power into a solid angle still carries the surface cosine; it is not uniform power per direction. For albedo 0.5 its BRDF is 0.5/pi, and a constant unit-radiance environment returns 0.5. For highlights, V points toward the camera and L toward the light. The half-vector H is the normalized sum V+L; it points between them. At a normal-facing camera and a light 60 degrees away, H is only 30 degrees from the normal. Blinn-Phong uses N dot H, unlike reflected-vector Phong.

A larger exponent makes a narrower, taller highlight. This conventional approximate scale is not an energy guarantee. With exponent 2 and normal view, c squared=(1+z)/2 where z=N dot L. Integrating over light directions gives 25/24, about 4.17 percent too much. Our test keeps that failure visible. Do not substitute this classic approximation for the conserving principled model.

2. Distribution, visibility and Fresnel are different factors

GGX D describes how microscopic surface normals are distributed. Its projected-area integral is one; this does not mean its raw values sum to one or that it is a complete BRDF. Perceptual roughness r maps to alpha=r squared, so the numerator uses r to the fourth power. At r=1, D is 1/pi.

Height-correlated Smith visibility describes geometric masking and shadowing of those microscopic facets. It is not the scene's shadow map. Our visibility factor already includes division by 4 times the view cosine times the light cosine; never divide twice. At r=1 it reduces to 1/(2*(nV+nL)) in the positive hemisphere. Schlick Fresnel describes angular reflectance:

For F0=0.04 and c=0.5, F=0.07. At c=1 it is F0; at c=0 it is one. Multiply D, Smith visibility and F to obtain the single-scattering GGX specular BRDF. Under a unit environment, roughness one, normal view and F=1, its exact outgoing value is 1-log(2), approximately 0.30685. The missing energy is not a numerical bug: this model omits multiple scattering. The separately specified principled coupling assigns a residual matte budget; these elementary factors do not.

From a surface parameter to a lit pixel

The public classic material now combines albedo/pi and an explicitly weighted Blinn highlight. It normalizes the normal, view and incident directions, and returns a BRDF only on the active reflection hemisphere. Back-facing or exact-horizon pairs have zero values and zero first derivatives; two-sided shading requires an explicit normal flip. It remains an empirical material, not an energy-conserving substitute for principled shading.

Colour may come from a constant, interpolated face corners, or a sampled texture. Those operations stay in the fitting graph. Rebuild a learned texture's pyramid after an update instead of reusing an old detached graph. The public light integrator then multiplies the BRDF by incident light and one surface cosine; solid-angle samples also receive their quadrature weight exactly once. Coverage, occlusion and the background remain separate. For two-sided materials the integrator must receive the same oriented normal.

Inspect the public classic versus saved reference comparison. It checks linear image error on shared geometry, not anatomical quality, independent rasterization, principled-budget admission or Cycles fidelity.

From a budget curve to a complete material

The public principled operation combines GGX distribution, height-correlated Smith visibility and Schlick Fresnel with a reciprocal matte term. It uses directional residual losses directly, not one minus a rounded energy value. Both view/light losses and their cosine-weighted mean stay in the current autodiff graph. The immutable resource stores curve coefficients; it must not cache evaluated losses from a previous optimization step.

A digest proves which bytes were loaded, not whether their light budget is physically accurate. The first public resource lane is CPU float64 with at most 32 scalar/channel entries per query. The exact ggx-smith-loss-cpu-f64-v1 package table now has finite-profile acceptance: 80 reference checks, 80 directional triples, 16 averages and 192 furnace cases. This is measured evidence at fixed points, not proof at every possible input, and it does not qualify larger renderers or GPU execution. See the identity and loading tests. Loading unrecognized synthetic data requires allow_unverified, and using it in a material separately requires allow_experimental_budget. These flags preserve format, domain and workspace checks; they do not turn synthetic data into a physical model.

From one surface point to an image

A correct reflection formula must also survive being applied to many pixels. Our principled direct-image comparison uses the same saved geometry on both sides and an independent scalar shader. This isolates material correctness; it does not independently validate the rasterizer. Error panels divide linear colour differences by the fixed tolerance, rather than hiding errors with display gamma.

A preview only needs forward values. Fitting also retains a derivative graph and can require more memory: eight points fit the current forward slice, but not its complete-material backward estimate. The tests preserve that rejection and compare shared gradients on four points split into two-point calls. A forward-only viewer must reject training inputs rather than silently detach them. Image agreement is not a frame-rate, full training-memory or environment-lighting convergence claim.

Why an environment reference can fail even when a shader is correct

At grazing angles, reflection changes rapidly over a small set of incoming directions. Uniform angular samples may miss that structure. The reference therefore compares two independent sampling layouts and requires two successive refinements to agree. A plausible last answer is not enough. Clustering existing nodes near the difficult angles can help without increasing the sample budget or relaxing accuracy.

Under constant unit illumination, the reciprocal matte term has an exact integral: surface colour times the directional residual loss. Its cosine-weighted mean cancels its normalizing denominator. This is not plain Lambert colour, and the glossy integral must still be included. Integrating this known term exactly avoids asking a global quadrature to resolve every interpolation segment in the loss curve.

The environment-image progress page preserves failed numerical rules and the successful complete-material reference controls. It also separates accuracy from execution cost: a correct point can still be too expensive to repeat over a whole image. A passing reference is not a finished image renderer.

Custom materials receive only normalized active reflection pairs and explicitly packed parameter fields. They return a BRDF without light or cosine. Registries belong to the application; resolving once retains the chosen callable. Custom lights declare delta or solid-angle units and the integrator applies each weight once. Callback compatibility alone does not prove conservation, reciprocity, deterministic behavior or export support.

The experimental material comparison shows these operations on the same analytic sphere. Built-in/custom Lambert equality is a measured comparison; the two principled pictures use a deliberately synthetic budget and are not physical acceptance evidence. Explicit forward-only tiles keep this demonstration bounded; they are not proof of renderer-scale training memory or sustained frame rate.

3. Boundaries and gradients are part of the operation

Functions accept finite float32/64 tensors with explicit point and batch axes. They do not turn negative cosines into positive ones, normalize input vectors or broadcast a new scene silently. The material layer owns direction preparation and two-sided decisions. Roughness zero is a delta limit, not a tiny hidden epsilon. A positive value that loses a needed divisor in the chosen dtype is an explicit error. Empty and strided tensors are still valid layouts.

Smith returns zero at either horizon with zero branch derivatives. Blinn uses zero derivatives at zero cosine, including its special exponent-zero corner. These conventions avoid NaNs but do not claim smooth physics at a discontinuity. Lambert and Schlick retain their algebraic endpoint derivatives. Interior finite-difference tests are different evidence from endpoint policy tests.

Exercise: compute Schlick and distinguish two normalization tests

For F0=0.2 and c=0.5, F=0.225. A GGX projected-NDF integral of one tests microfacet area; a hemisphere BRDF integral at most one tests energy. Passing the first does not establish the second. At exponent 2 the classic approximate Blinn response gives 25/24, so it fails a strict energy ceiling.

Implementation boundary and evidence

These are executable Phase-0 recipes, not yet public gffx.shade APIs, a completed principled material, CUDA conformance or a compiler/export guarantee. The four-sphere plate uses analytic normals and a declared display transform, not mesh rendering.

Differentiating the energy accountant

A material optimizer must know more than how bright a highlight is. When roughness changes, the shiny part reflects a different fraction of the incoming light, so the matte part's remaining budget changes too. Computing a budget once and detaching it from autodiff gives the optimizer an incomplete derivative even if the displayed forward image looks plausible.

Our new reference uses fixed light directions and integration weights independent of roughness, Fresnel reflectance and view cosine. Autodiff passes through every term of that weighted sum. Only constant quadrature nodes are cached. This avoids differentiating a moving sample-rejection boundary, but it can need many samples to resolve a narrow highlight. It is a correctness tool, not the shipping fast path or a real-time claim.

At c=0.5 the reflected fraction is 1-0.5 log(3), about 0.450694. Its derivative is -log(3)+2/3, about -0.431946. The cosine-weighted average across views is 4(1-log(2))/3, about 0.409137. These are single-scattering specular values, not the complete principled material. White matte fills the residual in the exact coupled model.

Three different questions need three different tests

  1. Does the computation differentiate its own formula? Interior gradcheck tests this.
  2. Does that formula approximate the intended integral? Independent visible-normal quadrature checks held-out values; refined direct-grid finite differences check derivatives.
  3. Does the complete material conserve energy? The separate independent furnace must still pass. A graph of E plus 1-E being one proves only arithmetic, not the accuracy of E.

The first reference run failed two refinement checks; increasing quadrature precision fixed them without changing the limits. No finite test grid proves every roughness or grazing limit. Current derivative evidence uses scalar float64 CPU tensors and positive interior view cosines; world-normal derivatives, public RGB/batch layouts and fast approximations remain separate work.

Exercise: what does freezing the budget lose?

If white matte has budget 1-E, its derivative with respect to roughness must be the negative of the shiny budget's derivative. Freezing E makes that response zero. The total may still look correct at the original parameter value while giving the optimizer the wrong direction to move.

Material values meet the surrounding light

Colour, roughness and reflectance are fields on a surface. A field may be constant, interpolated from triangle corners, or sampled from a UV texture. The material receives the resulting values at each surface point, not an image filename or an instruction to guess texture channels.

Albedo has three linear RGB channels. A uniform specular or F0 scalar explicitly means grey; a per-point grey field keeps a trailing one-channel axis so three points cannot be confused with three colours. Classic uses a highlight strength and an explicit exponent. Principled uses roughness and normal-incidence reflectance F0; these are not interchangeable meanings of specular.

Sample perceptual roughness first, then square it to obtain alpha for GGX. Squaring before interpolation gives a different material. Two equal weights on roughness 0.2 and 0.8 give r=0.5, then alpha=0.25; averaging the two pre-squared values would give 0.34 instead.

Textures are already supported; material wiring must respect them

The existing sampler reads level 0 unless LOD or derivatives are supplied. Keep UV seams as face-corner attributes, interpolate UVs, then sample. Colour uses three channels; roughness and grey reflectance use separate one-channel maps. The current native sampler supports at most four channels per call. Our first five-channel fixture was rejected; splitting the maps keeps that implementation limit explicit. Invalid background fragments stay outside material evaluation: their zero-filled roughness is not a valid rough surface.

Lighting integration needs both a direction and its share of the sky

A quadrature weight represents a small solid angle, measured in steradians. It is not a PDF, point-light intensity, or a set of numbers that should be normalized to sum to one. Evaluate the incoming radiance and complete material response at each direction, then apply the surface cosine and solid angle exactly once:

N, V and L are unit directions in one coordinate system. The reference normalizes nonzero vectors explicitly, keeps signed SH reconstruction, and never adds shadows or display gamma. The cosine derivative is declared zero exactly at the horizon. A separate material evaluator must also handle its view-side boundary; this integration helper cannot infer it from samples.

Our nine SH numbers per colour describe incident radiance. Lambert's convenient band factors already integrate one particular cosine-shaped response. Applying them to the shiny-plus-coupled-matte material changes the model. A nonconstant sky, Li=1+0.5*z, exposes that shortcut in an analytic roughness-one control. Incoming radiance reaches 1.5, so an outgoing value above one here is not by itself an energy violation. The unit-white furnace remains a different test.

Exercise: why not normalize quadrature weights?

For a unit Lambert surface under unit radiance, the hemisphere integral of the cosine is pi. The BRDF is 1/pi, so reflected radiance is one. Rescaling all weights scales the answer; dividing hemisphere solid angles by their sum 2*pi would produce 1/(2*pi), not one.

Current evidence covers field preparation, native interpolation/texture-to-field gradients, and environment summation. It does not close general material evaluation, fast budget selection, two-sided rules, scene acceptance, CUDA or compilation/export.

A small table can still have gradients

Imagine measuring the shiny energy budget at a grid of roughness and viewing-angle settings, then answering nearby queries by interpolation. The saved numbers are constants, but the query coordinates are not. Moving a roughness value changes its interpolation weights, so autodiff can still see how the answer changes. That differs from detaching the answer after looking it up.

For example, endpoint budgets 0.1 and 0.8 give 0.24 at F0=0.2, with derivative 0.7. The F0 interpolation is exact for this model; interpolation across roughness and view cosine is an approximation. The current trial uses a local three-by-three quadratic stencil, so values are continuous but slopes can change where the stencil changes. The old bilinear option remains selectable. A nice-looking value curve does not establish an accurate derivative.

The average is integrated exactly from each quadratic cosine segment times its cosine weight, using two Gauss nodes per interval. This keeps the two budget calculations consistent. It still does not prove the table agrees with the original GGX integral. We separately test held-out values and derivatives, then repeat the independent 108-case furnace without changing its limits.

Test the measuring stick as well as the shortcut

An expensive reference calculation is still a numerical approximation. Before blaming a table, increase the reference resolution and check whether its value and derivatives settle down. If they do not, the result is an unresolved reference, not evidence that the shortcut is accurate or inaccurate. Our expanded checks separate this guard from the table's own accuracy limits.

In the glossy, grazing-angle examples, uniformly spaced azimuth samples miss a narrow reflection peak. The integrand depends on azimuth through its cosine, so we can integrate half the circle and double the measure. A fixed Gauss grid concentrates samples near the endpoints, resolving that peak with fewer samples. The coordinates stay independent of the material parameters, so ordinary autodiff still applies. We keep the old rule as a negative control and compare the refined values with a separate visible-normal integration.

See the two angular grids converge differently. An improved reference can expose a real table error that was previously hidden by an unreliable comparison; it does not automatically make the table pass.

The next experiment doubled the angle samples and shared geometric integration work between the two Fresnel endpoints. It fixed the original error, but more grazing queries exposed three failures. Redistributing roughness knots then made sixteen checks fail, including the furnace refinement check. Neither failure was solved by relaxing a tolerance. Local quadratic interpolation on uniform roughness knots passes the expanded screening with the same stored sample count. It reads nine endpoint pairs per query instead of four. Quadratic interpolation is not generally shape-preserving: a finite dense energy-range screen supplements, but does not replace, the furnace and reference checks. These results do not prove accuracy everywhere between the test points.

Internal gradcheck asks whether autodiff differentiates the implemented approximation correctly. Reference comparison asks whether that approximation has the right physical slope. These are different questions. At a table knot, compare the declared one-sided slope instead of pretending there is a unique two-sided derivative. Finally, test the complete shiny-plus-matte response: normalizing directions and coupling both energy budgets must keep their chain-rule contributions. A deliberately detached budget is a useful wrong-answer control.

Scope is part of correctness

This candidate covers roughness 0.2 through 1, not zero roughness or every sharper material. Queries outside it fail rather than clamping. Gffx's physical domain has not been narrowed: a strategy for sharper materials must be resolved before adopting a public implementation. The table is currently a CPU development object, not an installed package resource, GPU result or compile/export guarantee.

The default candidate stores 138544 bytes of float64 knot, endpoint and average tensors (33 roughness by 257 cosine knots, plus axes and means), excluding Python object overhead and query temporaries. Expensive generation happens explicitly, once per constructed object; it must not run in a frame loop. Local timing records separate construction, batched queries and backward passes. They are not rendering frames per second.

Exercise: can constant table data give a nonzero gradient?

Yes. Interpolating values 2 and 6 over coordinates 0 and 1 gives 2+4*x. The data are constants, but its derivative with respect to x is 4. Detaching the final interpolated result would instead lose that derivative. At a knot, a piecewise-linear table needs a declared one-sided slope convention.

One low-precision generation produced 1.0000000000000013 at a unit-Fresnel horizon. The out-of-range guard rejected that rounding result; it was not clamped into acceptance. The historical rejection is retained while higher-precision generation and deterministic injected-error tests check the intended guard. Neither incident proves physical overreflection.

Polished surfaces: move the coordinates, not the material

A very smooth surface reflects light into a tiny angular region. A regular grid can step over that region entirely. Making the surface rougher would make integration easier, but would change the material we promised to evaluate. Instead, choose coordinates that follow its reflection.

Describe a microfacet's half-vector by its slope t and azimuth. Let c be the view cosine, and b the view's tangential component along that azimuth. A reflected ray is above the surface when:

Scale the slope by alpha=r squared, then use an angle beta with t=alpha*tan(beta). This concentrates integration around the narrow GGX peak. The largest allowed beta depends on the view and roughness. Keep that changing boundary in the autodiff graph: freezing it would discard part of the derivative. Constant unit-interval Gauss nodes are mapped through that boundary.

A second, independent visible-normal integration initially failed to converge in three comparison cases. Redistributing its radius-squared samples toward the unit-disk edge resolves those cases without adding samples or relaxing the limits. The old rule remains selectable and its failure is a regression control. Agreement matters only when both measuring methods are resolved.

The sharper reference passes sixty sampled value/gradient comparisons at roughness 0.01 through 0.199 and a separate 108-case shiny-plus-matte energy study. Its average is integrated over view directions, including roughness and Fresnel gradients. Exact roughness-one controls and a mirror-limit example check different parts of the calculation. These are finite tests, not a proof for every positive roughness or a completed public material.

The old fast table still rejects roughness below 0.2. A reliable offline reference is the measuring stick for its eventual extension, not an excuse to run expensive integration inside every pixel. Near-perfect reflection also leaves a tiny matte budget: subtracting almost equal numbers and dividing by that small remainder needs explicit conditioning checks.

When almost no light is left

If reflected energy E is almost one, the leftover 1-E can be billions of times smaller than the total. An error that looks harmless for E can dominate that tiny remainder. Dividing by an unresolved mean remainder can then change a matte budget substantially. A small absolute error is not enough: compare the error to the remainder itself, and check an independent integration method.

The first finite screen passed its sampled edge-on directional checks but failed five of six tiny remaining-budget cases. Redistributing views improved self-refinement, yet the old visible-normal sampler still disagreed. An exact normal-view control explains a concrete failure: that finite grid counts zero rejected reflections where their actual probability is one in a trillion.

The repair measures lost light directly. Under the normalized visible-normal distribution, loss is the probability of reflection below the surface plus the absorption and masking loss of valid reflections. The rejected tail has an analytic integral; the other terms are evaluated without subtracting near-unit quantities. We retain the tiny result as a separate value, not as one minus a rounded reflected-energy total. Two slope coordinates, independent direct tail integration, exact controls and gradient checks support the declared finite repair. The two coordinate schemes share the same physical identity: they are not two independent physical models or a proof for every positive roughness.

Exercise: if the true leftover is 0.00000001 and the reflected-energy estimate has absolute error 0.000000001, what is the relative error in the leftover? It is ten percent, despite the very small absolute error.

Inspect the magnified residual diagnostic and the boundary checks and their history. Inspect direct-loss acceptance and retained failure controls.

Approximating a tiny positive quantity

Storing the logarithm of a positive light loss lets an interpolation work with relative changes instead of trying to subtract almost-equal reflected energies. Interpolating between logarithms and exponentiating produces a geometric blend: inside a cell it stays between the positive corner values. The two Fresnel endpoint losses are then blended linearly, because this model is affine in Fresnel reflectance.

This is not a free accuracy guarantee. Values and derivatives must still be compared against the reference. A tiny local cell can pass while a practical full table fails. The local experiment has no complete angular domain or consistent integrated mean yet, so it cannot establish the coupled material's energy conservation. Inspect the local interpolation experiment.

One curve, one consistent average

The next experiment extends the curve from edge-on to straight-on views. Its average is computed from that exact curve after roughness interpolation, not from a second independently interpolated table. Between positive cosine knots, a straight line in log coordinates is a power law. Its cosine-weighted integral is analytic; a special stable limit handles the exponent that gives a logarithm.

The horizon cannot be a logarithmic knot because its cosine is zero. A separate limiting formula supplies its value, and the first segment is linear. At unit Fresnel reflectance the horizon loss is exactly zero; at normal view and roughness one it is log(2). Finite differences check roughness derivatives, and independent segment quadrature checks the analytic mean and its derivatives.

Worked example: if L(c)=c squared, the mean is twice the integral of c cubed, or one half. Replacing the first interval [0,b] by its linear endpoint segment adds b to the fourth power divided by six to this mean. That small, computable change illustrates why exact interpolation integrals and exact physics are different claims.

Exercise: can an exact average of an inaccurate curve still be inaccurate? Yes. Internal consistency prevents two parts of the material from disagreeing, but cannot make the curve physically correct. Directional, derivative, mean and white-furnace screens remain separate admission requirements. A failed grid stays experimental even if its white-furnace check passes. Inspect full-angle accuracy checks and the finite error-map demonstration.

Curved interpolation without invented light

The power-segment grid exposed two different problems: interpolating across roughness caused its remaining value errors, while angular interpolation caused a slope error. A replacement uses cubic curves whose control points stay between their endpoint values. Evaluating a Bezier curve forms convex combinations of those controls, so a nonnegative control polygon cannot create a negative loss.

The two Fresnel fields also need ordered control points; separately bounding each field is not enough to guarantee their ordering. A shared slope limit keeps their controls ordered. Across roughness we interpolate log loss; across angle we interpolate loss as a cubic in log cosine. That last distinction keeps the cosine-weighted mean analytically integrable with exponential-polynomial weights.

Worked example: controls 0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4 give value0.25 at the middle because the weights there are 1/8,3/8,3/8,1/8. The curve stays inside [0.1,0.4]. But these controls could still describe the wrong physical response: bounds are not an accuracy proof. Fresh parameter combinations, physical gradients and white-light energy checks remain separate requirements.

The first horizon segment stays linear. Later positive knots have continuous first derivatives, but neither the first junction nor limiter transitions promise unrestricted higher-order smoothness. Inspect the cubic control and integral tests and the separate physical screens.

Accurate does not automatically mean interactive

Prerequisite: distinguish fixed knot data from differentiable queries. Generating knots, loading them, constructing constants and evaluating a curve are different costs. Packing constants into tensors avoids Python object overhead, but does not prove a faster shader or a smaller backward graph.

Worked example: a two-by-three grid with two Fresnel endpoints stores 2+3+2*2*3=17 numbers. At eight bytes per double that is136 bytes before slopes, weights or container overhead. Exercise: what changes if three queries share it? Answer: constants can still occupy136 bytes; query temporaries and saved graphs grow separately. Sharing does not authorize detaching roughness-dependent means.

The bounded laptop experiment evaluates1,8,32 points in a scalar loop and measures backward separately. It is not a vectorized shader or frame-rate guarantee. Even the monitor needs tests: Windows can launch the actual Python worker behind a tiny redirector. Watching the redirector undercounts memory. Match measured and monitored process IDs, retain failures and keep time/byte limits explicit. See the measurement safeguard tests. The physical model, boundary derivatives and accuracy limits are unchanged.

Batch the arithmetic, not the evidence

Within one material call, a roughness curve can serve the view, many lights and all three colour channels. Its two Fresnel endpoint losses are mixed per channel afterward. This removes duplicate work without storing a stale graph between fitting steps. The derivative contributions still add at the shared roughness. Near the horizon, evaluate a linear segment as y0 + u*(y1-y0): its slope subtracts close endpoints before dividing by the tiny interval width, instead of cancelling huge derivative terms. See the reuse and derivative tests. The separately qualified CPU material lane now accepts1024 point/light pairs, at most8 forward or4 backward points, under the same64MiB planning ceiling. Standalone resource queries remain limited to32 entries. This is an explicit capacity contract, not automatic hidden tiling or a whole-image guarantee. See the batch boundary and gradient tests.

From one correct point to a checked image

A correct grazing-angle sample does not certify the other pixels. Our first full environment-image profile uses uniform unit light, fixed material parameters and the existing 128-by-128 head buffers. Each of its 6536 covered pixels needs its own converged reference: two angular partitions must agree, and two successive refinements must stay within the same tolerance. The public shader still integrates the full material; an exact reference identity is not permission to replace the candidate with an analytic image fill.

Tiles make the work stoppable, not automatically correct. Assembly rejects missing tiles, duplicated pixels and failed workers. Background pixels remain exactly zero. Saved estimates are rechecked instead of trusting a green status flag. Exercise: if 51 of 52 tiles pass, is the image accepted? No: it is partial evidence, even if the missing tile looks small. See the full-image and replay tests and the finite comparison page. Nonuniform environments and gradients through complete images require additional tests.

A stopped run can still contain valid completed tiles. Continuing it requires an explicit new work budget and verification of the original hashes, source identity, pixel ownership and convergence histories. The old stop remains in the record; its elapsed time is not reset. Only missing tiles execute, and the final image is accepted after all tiles pass together. See the checkpoint continuation tests. Reusing a verified numerical result is different from calling it a fresh experiment.

When the room is not equally bright in every direction

A simple coloured environment gives each RGB channel a preferred world direction. Its incoming radiance is one plus the dot product between a small colour-direction vector and the incoming unit direction. A vector shorter than one guarantees positive light everywhere. Rotating the object alone changes its lighting; rotating both the object and environment together must preserve it.

Uniform lighting let us double one half of the azimuth circle. Here that shortcut would give the wrong colours, so both halves are sampled explicitly. For a Lambert surface the integral is albedo times one plus two thirds of the colour vector's projection on the normal. The principled matte component instead needs an additional cosine-weighted moment of its residual loss curve. The average loss alone is not enough.

Both moments are independently integrated on the curve segments and require two successful refinements. This identity applies to affine illumination, not arbitrary HDR images. Exercise: why is rotating only the camera not equivalent to rotating the whole scene? The normal, view and fixed world-light directions have changed relative to one another. Inspect the world-lighting tests and the finite point-response demo. Passing selected points is preparation for a complete image, not a substitute for it.

Reuse constants, not answers

For a fixed material, the curve and its moments M and J do not depend on the pixel normal or viewing direction. A measuring worker can prepare its own copy once, then integrate each pixel separately. It must still check both angular estimates and both convergence transitions at every pixel. This is setup reuse, not interpolation between tested points and not a cache of differentiable graphs.

The selected-tile qualification measures three preselected tiles per material, including the short final tile. The tile diagram marks measured pixels green and everything else gray. Those 264 pixels per material are not an image-wide accuracy proof, nor a proven upper runtime bound for the remaining pixels. Exercise: which data may be reused when roughness changes? The geometry may stay fixed, but material-dependent moments must be recomputed.

From selected tiles to complete images

A completed tile is a durable checkpoint, not permission to call the whole picture correct. The full-image procedure owns every remaining tile exactly once, verifies the saved checkpoints, and assembles the two complete images only after all surface pixels pass. Each batch has its own work limit; cumulative time and failed attempts remain visible instead of resetting the history. The full-image evidence page shows a finite snapshot. Gray means uncomputed in that snapshot, never a correct black pixel. The final black background is accepted only after checking coverage.

Exercise: does a smooth-looking image with one missing tile pass? No. Visual plausibility does not establish complete ownership, numerical error or convergence.

Moving a resource is not qualifying a device

Before changing the execution device, also distinguish lighting from surface colour. Albedo is the surface's RGB diffuse reflectance: a checker changes this colour across the mesh, not the shape or the environment. At fixed geometry and roughness, both present materials have a diffuse term linear in albedo and a separate glossy contribution. Doubling albedo doubles only the diffuse part, not the whole reflected colour. Black diffuse paint can still have a highlight.

The saved-colour preflight uses vertex colours, a gradient texture and a checker texture at eight preselected surface points under two environments, for both materials: 96 comparisons. Every changed colour gets its own convergence history. Only fixed material moments are shared within a worker. The colour swatches separate input albedo, independent reflected colour and public output. These are samples, not complete textured images or tests of rasterized boundaries.

Exercise: why can a colour field reuse material moments while a new roughness cannot? The moments describe the roughness-dependent angular loss. Albedo scales the diffuse contribution after those moments have been computed.

Next, expand from selected points to prospectively selected image tiles. The textured-tile tests own the first, middle and short final tile for each of twelve profiles. Six serial batches measure3168 pixel/profile comparisons, but only264 of6536 surface pixels in each image. A saved tile contains the actual pixel IDs and colours, not just a green status. Duplicate or missing ownership invalidates the aggregate. In the partial-image view, gray means uncomputed, including background. This measures correctness and cost for the selected slices; it is not a guaranteed time bound for all remaining pixels.

A larger batch is not automatically faster

The material call allows at most 1,024 point/light pairs. One surface point can therefore use 1,024 light directions in a call; eight points can use only 128 each. Both layouts process the same number of pairs, so more points do not automatically mean fewer calls. They can change memory access, setup cost and the order of floating-point sums. The sampling tests keep each point's accepted integration order, directions, weights and world frame. Both estimates must match the independent reference and the saved public result.

The finite timing comparison uses identical outer timing boundaries, including validation. It alternates which method runs first, excludes one warmup and shows the median of three repetitions. Accuracy passing is separate from speed improving. A slower candidate is useful evidence to keep the earlier path, not a reason to relax numerical or memory limits.

A new pixel has no previous answer

A regression test can compare today's public result with yesterday's saved result. A newly tested pixel has no yesterday result. Copying its independent reference into a field called a previous result would invent evidence. Instead, the reference-only tests validate the exact material, environment, surface colour and geometry, then compare two fresh public angular estimates with that pixel's independently converged reference. The old saved results are used only for separate regression checks.

The continuation view fills in verified tiles without rerunning the original checkpoints. Each pixel keeps its own convergence history even when several pixels share a bounded public call. Gray means uncomputed, not black shading. All52 tiles belong to one image, and all12 profiles require624 tiles; progress is not full-image acceptance.

Once all tiles for one profile exist, the complete-image checks place every measured colour at its exact pixel, leave the declared background at zero, and recompute the image error. Saved image bytes must reconstruct exactly from those checkpoints. This closes one image profile, not the eleven others. Testing shader colours on shared geometry buffers also does not independently validate rasterization or prove that an image loss has correct gradients.

The same table can be transferred explicitly to a GPU without granting it the CPU acceptance record. First compare values and derivatives, then independently check physical accuracy, energy, repeated calls and memory on that device. The experimental CUDA tests separate these claims. A process-memory stop is neither a passing energy test nor evidence that the material creates energy. Host working set, GPU allocations and GPU reserved memory are different measurements; importing and initializing a framework also consumes host memory. A limit must be changed explicitly, not hidden by omitting initialization from the measurement.

A tensor-resident resource shares fixed constants while evaluating many queried roughnesses and angles. Shared Fresnel parameters receive the sum of each point's derivative. The mean must still be the integral of the same curve, not a detached lookup. Exercise: if two points contribute derivatives0.2 and0.3 to one shared parameter, what is its total derivative? Answer:0.5, provided the objective is their sum; averaging the objective would instead give0.25.

Our internal batch candidate passes scalar value/gradient parity and the existing directional physical comparisons. Its first independent mean-validation worker reached the unchanged process memory ceiling and was stopped; furnace checks were initially not run. That was a resource-validation stop, not a measured violation of energy conservation. The reference retained64 full viewing-angle graphs. A validation-only repair now takes each weighted view's first derivatives before releasing its graph, then sums the finished measurements. The same36 mean and396 furnace regressions pass under the original process cap. No physical samples or accuracy limits were removed. See batch and loading checks and the physical validation page. Allocator peak, float32, GPU and compilation remain separate claims.

Differentiate a finite sum without keeping every graph

Let q_i(theta) be one weighted viewing-angle contribution and theta denote roughness or Fresnel reflectance. For a finite sum, the derivative of the sum is the sum of the derivatives. Compute each q_i and its derivative, keep those small numbers, and release the intermediate graph before the next view. Crucially, differentiate the entire contribution: the transformed viewing angle and its integration weight can also depend on roughness. Detaching those early changes the answer. Our test helper returns first-partial measurements, not a reusable autodiff function or a higher-derivative guarantee.

Exercise: if q_1(theta)=theta squared and q_2(theta)=3 theta, what value and derivative should be recorded at theta=2? Answer: value10 and derivative7. Computing the two derivatives separately gives4+3=7. Discarding the graph only after taking each derivative preserves that result. The saved-reference diagnostic and original-oracle comparisons are explained on the memory validation page.

More useful samples, not merely more samples

A later nearly edge-on check exposed a different problem: the generated knot itself needed better angular integration. Doubling the radial samples did not help; doubling the azimuth samples did. The experiment reallocates the same budget below cosine = roughness squared / 16: 280 by 32 becomes 140 by 64. Normal views keep their radial resolution. This is a numerical sampling choice, not a new physical cutoff or permission to clamp the answer. We test both sides of that allocation boundary and preserve the original failed measurements.

Once a new validation point exposes a bug, it becomes development data. A second parameter cohort was declared before evaluating the revised candidate; rerunning it later is useful regression evidence, but is not fresh unseen validation. See the sampling checks.

Why does the polished-sphere picture not prove energy conservation?

The picture uses 512 deterministic environment samples per pixel, analytic spheres and an illustrative display transform. It can show reflection shape but can still have integration error. The energy tests separately integrate independent specular reflection plus the coupled matte response under a white environment and enforce the original numerical limits.

Check the checker before comparing images

The synthetic-head reference uses scalar standard-library equations, direct Hermite polynomials and adaptive integration over angular segments. It does not call the public shader or the tensor lookup implementation. First we compare this reference with linear and log-polynomial closed forms, including a changing roughness field. Then it can check shader values on shared input buffers. That shared-buffer test does not independently validate rasterization.

A synthetic budget can show that lookup values, means and material algebra are wired consistently; only separate physical integration can qualify energy conservation. Likewise, a synthetic fitting scene is not real-model qualification, and agreement with our declared equations is not a Cycles-quality claim. See the independent-reference tests and the public boundary checks.
